subject: music
title: Detroit techno: Music for a city after the factory (1980–1995)
dek: In the early 1980s three Black teenagers from the small town of Belleville, outside Detroit, mixed Parliament's funk with Kraftwerk's machines and Alvin Toffler's futurism. They called the result techno. This lesson follows the sound from Cybotron and the Electrifying Mojo's radio show to Strings of Life, the British rave boom, Underground Resistance and the Detroit–Berlin alliance, and looks at the man who started it, Juan Atkins, who died on 31 October 2026.
era: About 1980 to 1995, in Detroit and its suburbs, with roots in 1970s funk, disco and European synth-pop, and effects on rave culture in Britain, Berlin and the rest of the world
honesty: This lesson keeps to dates, names and events documented in the English Wikipedia articles Detroit techno, Techno, Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson, Cybotron, The Electrifying Mojo, Strings of Life, Underground Resistance, Jeff Mills, Drexciya, Carl Craig, Richie Hawtin, K-Hand, Roland TR-808, Roland TB-303, Second Summer of Love, Warp Records and Detroit, the Chinese Wikipedia article 抓狂歌, and the November 2026 obituaries of Juan Atkins in Billboard, the Detroit Free Press/USA Today and The Guardian. No cause of Atkins's death had been reported when this was written. The analysis sections are my own summary, not claims from a single source.

fun_fact.title: A record label named after a turntable slider
fun_fact.text: Richie Hawtin and John Acquaviva, working across the river in Windsor, Ontario, named their label Plus 8 after the pitch control on a Technics turntable, which lets a DJ speed a record up by at most 8 percent. They saw the label as a friendly rival to Underground Resistance and kept pushing their tracks faster and harder, as if they were always playing with the slider pushed to the top.

sections.title: Before techno: Motor City, funk and a radio show from space

blocks.text: Detroit was the capital of the American car industry and one of the richest cities in the United States in the middle of the twentieth century. Its population peaked at about 1.85 million in 1950. From the 1950s onward, factories moved to the suburbs and to other states, automation replaced many assembly-line jobs, and white families left for the suburbs. The 12th Street uprising of 1967, one of the deadliest and costliest civil disturbances in American history, sped up that departure. By the 1970s Detroit had a Black majority and a shrinking tax base, and by 2020 its population had fallen to about 639,000.

Detroit already had a world-famous musical history. Motown had turned local Black singers into international stars in the 1960s before moving to Los Angeles in the early 1970s, and George Clinton's Parliament and Funkadelic had built a whole science-fiction mythology around funk, complete with a stage-prop spaceship called the Mothership. Disco and then Chicago house showed that a DJ playing records for a dancing crowd could become a creative art of its own (see the disco and Chicago house lessons).

The most important single influence on the future techno producers was a radio DJ. Charles Johnson, known on air as the Electrifying Mojo, started broadcasting on WGPR in 1977 and moved to WJLB around 1982, where billboards announced the 'Landing of the Mothership' at 10 p.m. every night. Mojo ignored radio formats. He played entire albums without interruption, hours of Prince including deep cuts and B-sides, and put German electronic music by Kraftwerk next to funk, new wave and rock. Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson, Jeff Mills, Carl Craig and Richie Hawtin have all named him as an influence.

Juan Atkins was born in Detroit on 12 September 1962. His father was a concert promoter, and Atkins played guitar and bass in funk bands as a boy. When his parents separated he moved to his grandmother's house in Belleville, a small, mostly white town about 30 miles from downtown Detroit. At 15 or 16 he persuaded his grandmother to buy him a Korg MS-10 synthesizer, after hearing what Parliament did with keyboards. At school he met two younger boys: Derrick May, born in 1963 and raised by a single mother, and Kevin Saunderson, born in Brooklyn in 1964, who had moved to Belleville as a child.

The three became known as the Belleville Three. Atkins was the first to learn to mix records, and he taught the other two. They listened to an unusual mix of records: Kraftwerk, Yellow Magic Orchestra, Parliament, Bootsy Collins, Prince, Depeche Mode and the B-52's. May later said that the suburban setting changed how they heard it: 'We'd sit back with the lights off and listen to records by Bootsy and Yellow Magic Orchestra. We never took it as just entertainment, we took it as a serious philosophy.' Atkins and May DJed at parties under the name Deep Space Soundworks, and by 1981 Mojo was playing their mixes on the radio.

Their scene had a class dimension that later writers have examined closely. Early techno grew out of 'prep' parties thrown by the children of Black families who had prospered from the car industry. The parties had European-sounding names such as Plush, Charivari and GQ Productions, enforced dress codes, and sometimes put up signs saying 'No Jits', a slang insult for poorer inner-city youths. Techno began, in other words, as the music of a Black middle class that was looking to Europe and the future rather than to the street.

sections.title: Juan Atkins, Cybotron and the word 'techno'

blocks.text: At Washtenaw Community College Atkins met Richard Davis, who recorded as 3070, and in 1980 they formed Cybotron. They released their first single, Alleys of Your Mind, on their own Deep Space label in 1981, and it sold about 15,000 copies, mostly in Detroit. Two more singles, Cosmic Cars and Clear, persuaded the California label Fantasy to sign them, and their album Enter came out in 1983. Clear, a cold, precise electro track built on drum machine and synthesizers, is still regarded as one of the foundational records of Detroit electronic music.

The ideas behind the music came from the futurist writer Alvin Toffler, whose book Future Shock Atkins first read as the textbook for a high-school course called Future Studies. Future Shock (1970) and The Third Wave (1980) argued that industrial society was ending and an information society was beginning, and The Third Wave described 'techno-rebels' who would use the new technology for their own ends. Atkins took the words cybotron and metroplex from Toffler and began using the word techno for his music. One of Cybotron's singles was called Techno City. Atkins said that Detroit was the most advanced city in the world in the transition away from industrialism, so it was the natural place for music about what came next.

The duo split in 1985 over creative differences. Atkins founded his own label, Metroplex, and began recording as Model 500. His single No UFO's (1985) is usually treated as the first record of Detroit techno as a separate style: the funk is still there in the rhythm, but the sound is sparse, mechanical and slightly eerie. Metroplex also released early records by Eddie 'Flashin' Fowlkes, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson and Robert Hood. Writers later gave the three friends nicknames: Atkins the Originator, May the Innovator and Saunderson the Elevator.

Atkins died on 31 October 2026 at the age of 64. He was found unresponsive in a hotel room in Mexico City before a scheduled performance at the YuYu Cine Club and was pronounced dead at a hospital; his agency, Greensmith Artists, announced the news the next day. He had been touring until the end and had played in Amsterdam on 23 October. Detroit's mayor, Mary Sheffield, said he 'gave the world a new sound. As a teenager with a synthesiser and a big idea, he imagined what the music of the future could be. Then he built it.'

sections.title: Cheap Japanese machines that failed in the shops

blocks.text: Techno depended on a set of instruments that their makers considered commercial failures. The Japanese company Roland released the TR-808 drum machine in 1980. It was one of the first drum machines that let users program their own rhythms, but its analog sounds did not resemble real drums, and professional musicians mostly rejected it. Roland built only about 12,000 before stopping production in 1983 and replaced it with the TR-909. The TB-303 Bass Line of 1981, designed by Tadao Kikumoto to replace a bass guitarist, sounded nothing like a bass guitar and was discontinued in 1984.

Those failures were good news for young musicians in Detroit and Chicago, because the machines soon appeared cheaply in second-hand shops. The 808's booming bass drum became central to electro and hip-hop (see the hip-hop origins lesson), the 909 became the standard techno and house drum machine, and the squelching sound of a 303 being twisted beyond its intended use became acid house. A teenager in a basement with a drum machine, a synthesizer and a four-track recorder could now make a record without a band or a studio.

This is also a good example of why Detroit techno connected so easily with the rest of the world. Its producers were Black Americans using Japanese instruments to reinterpret German electronic music, and they were inspired as much by Yellow Magic Orchestra in Tokyo as by Kraftwerk in Düsseldorf (see the krautrock lesson). May once described Detroit techno as 'like George Clinton and Kraftwerk caught in an elevator, with only a sequencer to keep them company.'

sections.title: Derrick May, Strings of Life and the British rave boom

blocks.text: Derrick May had worked part-time in a video arcade as a teenager and travelled with Atkins and Saunderson to Chicago, where they studied the DJs Ron Hardy and Frankie Knuckles. In 1987 he founded the Transmat label and released Nude Photo, co-written with Thomas Barnett, under the name Rhythim Is Rhythim. His next record became the most famous techno track of all.

Strings of Life started with a piano ballad called Lightning Strikes Twice, which May's friend Michael James played at May's house. May sampled and chopped the piano part, layered synthetic string arrangements over a fast drum pattern, and gave a demo tape to Frankie Knuckles, who named the track. It has no conventional bassline, which puzzled some Chicago DJs, but on the dance floor its rushing strings sounded joyful rather than cold. It 'hit Britain in an especially big way' during the 1987–1988 house explosion, and Knuckles said it 'just exploded'. In 2015 LA Weekly ranked it the best dance music track in history.

Britain was where Detroit techno got its name and its first mass audience. In 1988, the Second Summer of Love, London clubs such as Shoom, Spectrum and Manchester's Haçienda were filled with crowds dancing to Chicago acid house, often on the drug ecstasy, and the smiley face became the scene's symbol. The Birmingham record man Neil Rushton, a former Northern Soul DJ scouting for Virgin's 10 Records imprint, contacted May to find out what was happening in Detroit. The compilation they made was going to be called The House Sound of Detroit, but after Atkins contributed a track called Techno Music, the Belleville Three voted against calling their music a regional kind of house. It came out in 1988 as Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit.

Kevin Saunderson profited most directly. His project Inner City came about almost by accident when a Chicago friend suggested the singer Paris Grey, who flew to Detroit and wrote lyrics for a track that became Big Fun. Rushton put it on the compilation, it became an international hit, and its follow-up, Good Life, sold even more. Over three albums Inner City had nine UK top 40 hits and sold more than six million records. Under another name, Reese, Saunderson made Just Want Another Chance (1988), whose growling 'Reese bass' was later copied throughout British jungle and drum and bass.

sections.title: The Music Institute, Underground Resistance and the second wave

blocks.text: Back home, techno needed a club. In 1988 Chez Damier, Alton Miller and George Baker opened the Music Institute at 1315 Broadway in downtown Detroit, modelled on Chicago's house clubs. May, Atkins and Saunderson played there with Eddie Fowlkes and Blake Baxter, and the club turned a scattered scene into what its regulars called a family. May remembered 'a young beautiful black crowd' and added, 'We had white kids coming, Spanish kids coming, gay kids coming, straight kids coming.' It was short-lived, but it trained the next generation. The three founders' labels, Metroplex, KMS and Transmat, all ended up on Gratiot Avenue near the Eastern Market, a strip nicknamed Techno Alley.

The second wave, from about 1989, was harder and angrier. Underground Resistance was formed in 1989 by 'Mad' Mike Banks and Jeff Mills, a radio DJ famous as 'the Wizard' for his fast mixing and scratching, and Robert Hood soon joined. UR presented itself as a paramilitary group fighting 'the programmers' of the commercial music industry, with track titles such as Riot, Predator, Elimination and Death Star. Its members performed in balaclavas behind a plain UR logo, partly to resist the 'superstar DJ' cult and partly to push back against the profiling of Black DJs. UR rejected the image of techno as drug music and set up Submerge, a business network of labels, musicians, lawyers and financial advisers meant to give Detroit artists an economic safety net. Mills and Hood left in 1992 to work solo, Mills founding Axis Records, while Banks kept UR going and explored jazz as Galaxy 2 Galaxy.

Other second-wave artists took the music in different directions. Carl Craig, born in 1969, founded Planet E and made techno that borrowed from jazz and soul. Across the river in Windsor, Ontario, the English-born Richie Hawtin and John Acquaviva founded Plus 8 in May 1990, and Hawtin later became a leader of minimal techno as Plastikman. The duo Drexciya, James Stinson and Gerald Donald, released records on UR and built one of the most powerful myths in electronic music. In the notes to their 1997 album The Quest they described Drexciya as an underwater nation of the unborn children of pregnant African women thrown overboard from slave ships, who had learned to breathe underwater in the womb. Stinson died of a heart condition in 2002.

Women were rare in the early scene, and the vocalist Paris Grey was its best-known female voice. Kelli Hand, known as K-Hand, changed that from the DJ booth. Born in Detroit in 1964, she taught herself to DJ and produce in her bedroom after spending her youth in New York clubs such as the Paradise Garage, founded her own label in 1990 (soon renamed Acacia Records after a Detroit street where she had lived), and released records on Warp and Tresor. She became known as the 'First Lady of Detroit techno' and is credited with opening the door for Black women in a male-dominated music. She died in 2021.

sections.title: What Detroit techno was really about

blocks.text: Detroit techno was music about the future made in a city that many Americans saw as having no future. The car factories that had employed its founders' parents were being automated, and robots were taking the jobs. The producers' answer was to take the same kind of technology and use it themselves. One writer described the process as taking technology and making it 'a black secret'. That is why techno is often discussed as part of Afrofuturism, the tradition, running from Sun Ra and Parliament to Drexciya, of Black artists using science fiction to imagine a different relationship with history and power.

It was also a music that wanted to escape racial labels, and that desire was complicated. Atkins said, 'to me it shouldn't be white or black music, it should be just music.' Yet the music was largely invisible in its own country. Detroit producers found their audiences in Britain, Germany, Belgium and Japan, while many Americans learned about techno only years later through European artists. Carl Craig said in 1993 that American artists sent their music to Europe because it was accepted there by a wider audience. When electronic dance music became a huge commercial industry in the 2010s, many of its best-known stars were white Europeans and Americans, and the Black Detroit origins were often overlooked.

Finally, the first and second waves represent two different politics. The first wave was aspirational and European-looking, born in suburban prep parties. The second wave, especially Underground Resistance, spoke from the perspective of the struggling inner city, treated independent record labels as a form of economic self-defence, and turned the music into protest. Both were responses to the same collapse of the industrial city.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: In Chicago, a few hours' drive away, house music was being born in the same years from the same ingredients: disco records, drum machines and a mostly Black and gay club audience (see the Chicago house lesson). The Belleville Three learned from Chicago, and British journalists at first described Detroit techno as Detroit's high-tech version of house.

In Britain, 1988 and 1989 brought acid house and the rave era, and by late 1988 the tabloid The Sun had turned from selling smiley T-shirts to running scare stories about drugs, a classic moral panic (see the moral panic lesson). In Sheffield, Warp Records was founded in 1989 and became associated with the 'bleep' sound of LFO and Sweet Exorcist, a British cousin of Detroit techno. Warp's 1992 compilation Artificial Intelligence helped invent electronic music for home listening, and in 1994 it released K-Hand's Global Warning.

In Germany, the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 left empty buildings across East Berlin, and illegal parties filled them. Tresor opened in 1991 in the vaults of a former department store near the old border and became the leading techno club, playing host to Eddie Fowlkes, Blake Baxter, Jeff Mills and Underground Resistance. Detroit had been shaped by deindustrialisation and Berlin by the end of the Cold War, but both were cities where young people made music in the ruins of an old order. Tresor's 1993 compilation was called Berlin & Detroit – A Techno Alliance.

In Taiwan, martial law ended in 1987, and popular music began to change quickly. In November 1989 Black List Studio (黑名單工作室) released 抓狂歌 (Songs of Madness) on Rock Records, an album sung almost entirely in Taiwanese that used rock, rap and reggae to describe taxi drivers, factory towns and corrupt politics. Critics treat it as the start of the 1990s New Taiwanese Song movement. Like Detroit techno, it was music by young people who rejected the official soundtrack of their society and used new styles to describe how ordinary lives had changed (see the Taiwan campus folk lesson for the movement it was reacting against).

sections.title: After Detroit: from rave to festival stage

blocks.text: By the mid-1990s techno was a global genre with its own subgenres, labels and festivals, and Berlin had become its second capital. Several Detroit producers lived there for a time, Jeff Mills among them, and Berlin's Basic Channel label had its records mastered at National Sound Corporation in Detroit. In 2000 the first Detroit Electronic Music Festival brought fans from around the world to Hart Plaza on the Detroit River. Derrick May took over the festival in 2004 and lost a great deal of his own money on it, and it has continued under the name Movement.

The founders' later lives were mixed. Atkins kept releasing music as Model 500, including Deep Space (1995), and kept touring until the week he died. Saunderson continued Inner City and KMS. May largely stopped releasing records in the 1990s but kept DJing around the world; in November 2020 several women accused him of sexual assault dating back to the early 2000s, which he denies. Underground Resistance still runs from Detroit, and the generation of artists it influenced, from Berlin's techno clubs to hyperpop producers using cheap software (see the hyperpop lesson), still works with the idea that a young person with a machine can invent a new sound.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Detroit techno was invented by Black producers but became famous through European clubs and labels, and its origins were often forgotten when it made money. If cool dairy sells vintage clothes with stories attached, how will it make sure the women and communities behind those stories are credited, and benefit, rather than just being used as decoration?
